opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that without reasoning, models were being forced to answer everything in a single shot. You'd give them a problem, and they'd have to produce the answer immediately, token by token, with no room to think. And that's just not how hard problems get solved. If you asked a person to solve a complex math problem or debug a piece of code without letting them pause, scribble, try something, realize it's wrong, and backtrack, they'd fail too.

So reasoning gives the model the ability to spend more compute on harder problems. A trivial question like "what's the capital of France" shouldn't take the same effort as "help me restructure this financial model" or "figure out why this system is failing." Before, we were spending the same amount of compute per token regardless of difficulty, which is a strange design when you think about it. Reasoning lets the model allocate effort proportionally.

The other big piece is robustness. When a model can lay out its steps, check its own work, notice an error, and correct course, you get far fewer of those confident, wrong answers. For enterprise use cases, which is where we spend most of our time at Cohere, that's essential. Businesses need to trust the output. They need agents that can take multi-step actions, call tools, see that a tool returned something unexpected, and adapt rather than just plowing ahead.

And frankly, it unlocks a whole category of tasks that were previously out of reach. Agentic workflows, where a model has to plan, execute, observe, and replan, basically depend on reasoning. Without it, you have a very impressive autocomplete. With it, you start to have something that can actually do work on your behalf.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning lets models spend more compute on harder problems and allocate effort proportionally to difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think reasoning is essential because it's really the difference between a model that pattern-matches and a model that can actually do work.

If you look at the first generation of language models, they were essentially giving you a single-shot answer. You put in a prompt, and whatever came out was the model's best guess from one forward pass. That works surprisingly well for a lot of tasks, but it falls apart the moment a problem requires multiple steps, or where the model needs to check its own work, or where the first intuition is simply wrong. Humans don't operate that way. When you're solving a hard problem, you think, you try something, you notice it didn't work, you back up and try again. Reasoning is giving the model that same capacity to spend compute proportional to the difficulty of the problem.

The second reason is reliability, which is the thing enterprises actually care about. Our customers aren't asking whether a model can write a poem. They're asking whether it can take a messy, multi-step task, go through documents, call tools, reconcile contradictory information, and land on a correct answer consistently. That's fundamentally a reasoning problem. A model that can decompose a task, plan, execute, and verify is far more trustworthy than one that just produces fluent text, even if the fluent text is right most of the time.

And the third piece is that reasoning is what unlocks agents. If you want a model to go do things in the world, to operate over hours rather than seconds, you need it to be able to maintain a chain of thought, recover from errors, and know when it's uncertain. Without that, you get a very impressive demo that breaks in production.

So I see it less as a feature and more as the foundation. Knowledge in a model is table stakes now. The thing that separates a useful system from a toy is whether it can reason over that knowledge to get something done.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning lets a model “spend compute proportional to the difficulty of the problem,” directly conveying that effort varies with problem complexity.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning is what lets a model move beyond things it has already seen. You want it to encounter a new problem, work through the constraints, and arrive at an answer—even when there isn’t some example it can reproduce from training.

And a lot of useful work requires that. If you’re writing code or helping someone make a decision, the answer usually isn’t a single fact. You have to connect pieces of information, consider alternatives, and check whether your conclusion actually follows.

The exciting part is being able to spend more computation on a harder problem. Instead of having to produce an answer immediately, the model can work through it and revise its approach. That doesn’t automatically make it correct, but it gives us a way to tackle problems that need more than an immediate response.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can spend more computation on a harder problem, clearly linking computational effort to problem complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reasoning is essential because so many of the things we want models to do require more than producing an immediate answer. They require working through a problem, noticing when an assumption is wrong, and trying a different approach.

If you ask a model to help solve a difficult coding problem, for example, you want it to break the problem down, consider possible solutions, and check whether its answer actually works. You don’t just want something that sounds plausible.

And there’s a limit to how much of that you can do in a single, immediate response. Some problems need more computation than others. Reasoning gives models a way to spend more effort on the hard cases. That’s a really important step toward systems we can trust with more complex work.

r001.rationale: The response says some problems need more computation than others and reasoning lets models spend more effort on hard cases.
